PI: Rebecca Brooker, PhD We leverage team expertise in developmental science, a novel aperiodic slope measure, and overlapping neuroimaging techniques to demonstrate and validate aperiodic slope as a usable proxy for neural maturation across a critical period of neurodevelopment.
Contact
PI: Rebecca Brooker, PhD
  • rebeccabrooker@tamu.edu

Overview

This project is being used to develop a novel metric of neurodevelopment, demonstrating its links to psychological constructs that support healthy emotional development during childhood.  Children and 1 parent will participate in two laboratory visits, each lasting approximately 60 minutes. Psychometric Properties of a Brief Value Driven Attention Task

PI: Brian Anderson, PhD Co-I – Steven Woltering, PhD The current study investigates the psychometric properties of a brief attention assessment using eye-tracking technology.  
Contact
Jacob Brooks
  • jtbrooks@tamu.edu

Overview

The primary purpose of this study is to investigate the psychometric properties of a brief attention assessment using eye tracking task. At times, previously reward-associated or otherwise motivationally significant stimuli are difficult to ignore even when a person knows that they are irrelevant to the current task, reflecting an involuntary attentional bias acquired through learning. This influence of reward on attention is typically measured using an hour-long assessment, and the present study tests whether it is possible to reliably measure this influence using a much quicker assessment. A secondary purpose of the study is to investigate whether this attentional bias is related to behaviors in everyday life assessed via questionnaire and to reward’s influence on memory.

To be eligible, participants must be: 

  1. Age 18-35 (inclusive)
  2. English speaking
  3. Have normal or corrected-to-normal (e.g., glasses, contacts) visual acuity
  4. Have normal color vision
  5. Must not be allergic to any of the ingredients in M&Ms (including sugar, milk, cocoa, peanut, hazelnut, and almond). Note that the M&Ms used do not contain peanut, hazelnut, and almond as ingredients but are processed in a factory that uses such ingredients, and so are also included as potential allergens.
  6. Must not have anything to eat for at least 3 hours leading up to the experiment. 

Duration

55 minutes across two lab visits (35 minutes for visit 1; 20 minutes for visit 2). 

Compensation

Up to $20: Participants are compensated $5 per lab visit in the form of a gift card. Each participant will have an opportunity to earn an additional $5 during each lab visit for task-related reward.

title.rendered: Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

content.rendered:
1. Home
  2. Aggie Research Volunteers
  3. Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

PI: Jessica Bernard, PhD This work is seeking to understand how the hormonal changes and fluctuations of perimenopause impact how brain networks are organized, and in turn how hormone therapy may impact these networks and their changes. We are using a technique called dense sampling with brain imaging, where we will take a lot of measurements (24) over time, in a sample of 8 dedicated women, to better understand how this dynamic time of change impacts the brain in middle-aged and older women.
Contact
Jessica Bernard
  • 979-845-2581
  • Jessica.bernard@tamu.edu

Overview

During perimenopause levels of hormones such as estrogen are fluctuating in the body, and this can lead to cognitive dysfunction, including brain fog, which impacts women’s quality of life. The brain relies on large-scale networks – connections among brain areas – to support cognition. Despite growing evidence suggesting estrogen’s role in brain network organization, research on how hormonal fluctuations impact brain connectivity during menopause is limited. Additionally, hormone therapy (HT) remains controversial, with uncertainty about the optimal timing for its initiation to preserve brain health and prevent neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s. This project aims to explore how estrogen fluctuations during menopause impact brain network connectivity and to evaluate the effects of HT on these changes.

Using resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI), a type of brain imaging where participants relax and let their mind wander, we will examine the impact of menopause and HT on the dynamic functional connections in the brain. This study will use dense-sampling approaches (many longitudinal measures on small samples, in this case, 24 measures across 6 months) to investigate fluctuations in brain network connectivity in humans at different menopausal stages (perimenopause and post-menopause), with and without HT. All participants will undergo weekly brain imaging scans scheduled at the participant’s convenience, provide saliva samples at each visit to measure hormones, answer questionnaires related to menopausal symptoms and health, and wear an Oura ring to track sleep, heart rate, body temperature, and movement. Only females will be included in this study, and participation is limited to 4 participants: 2 perimenopausal participants, and 2 post-menopausal participants. One participant in each category will be using HT and the other will not. There are no strict age limits or exclusions, but we expect that all participants will be over the age of 40. Exclusion criteria include left-handedness and any factor that is a contraindication for the brain imaging environment. 

Duration

Participants will complete 24 visits. These visits will be once per week over the course of 6 months. 

Compensation

Participants will be compensated $20 per visit. They will also receive a completion bonus of $500 for completing all visits, totally $1000. Finally, participants will be asked to wear an Oura ring for the 6-months of the study. After the study is complete they will be able to keep the ring.

Investigating the trust of video messages using Dial Smith (Phase 1 of Agriculture Video Messaging Project)

PI: Dr. Holli Leggette, PhD in agriculture discipline The purpose of this study is to use Dial Smith technology to investigate trust and perception at Texas A&M University based on videos regarding beef from gene-edited cattle, milk and conservation friendly agricultural practice. The aim of the study is to examine video framing effect.
Contact
Holli Leggette
  • Holli.Leggette@ag.tamu.edu

Overview

Study Procedures: The experiment will be through continuous response measurement (CRM) and self-report measures. Each participant will watch one videos about milk production five times. Instead of using traditional self-reported survey to measure trust, we utilize Dial Smith technology to measure trustworthy. Each time watching the video, participant will focus on and evaluate one dimension of trust. Participants will be asked to conduct an evaluation based on their perceptions of the trust construct under five dimensions: trust, honest, dependability, reliability and sincerity. Participants will be asked to continuously indicate their agreement or disagreement with the assigned prompt using a CRM tool called a dial. With all dials set at 50 to begin, participants then use their dial to indicate their evaluation of the messages in the video by turning their dial to the left or right. The far left of the dial, which is set at 0, indicated “strongly disagree” and the far right of dial, set at 100, indicates “strongly agree.” Each time the video last 2 minutes, so in total participants will be exposures to video about 10 minutes in total.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria: The Participants have to be over the age of 18. They need to be students at Texas A&M University. They need to be a consumer. Phase 1 will involve participant. We will not involve adults unable to consent. There will be no minors involved. There will be no pregnant women involved. There will be no prisoners involved.

Actuatable Footrest for Sit-Stand Desks: Evaluation of Control Interfaces, Usability, and Sensor-Based Usage Measurement

PI: Mark E. Benden, PhD, CPE
Professor and Head, Environmental & Occupational Health, Texas A&M University This study evaluates a novel actuatable footrest for sit-stand desks. We will compare control interfaces, assess usability compared to conventional footrests, and validate a contactless sensor system to measure workstation use. Findings aim to improve ergonomic design and worker health.
Contact
Pronob Kumar Biswas
  • 979-326-7597
  • pronob@tamu.edu

Overview

We are conducting a study to learn how a new office footrest can improve health and comfort when people use sit-stand desks. Traditional footrests must be manually repositioned for every sit-to-stand or stand-to-sit transition, but this new footrest moves at the press of a button, making it easier to use. Our goal is to find out which type of controller is easiest to operate the footrest, whether this new design feels more comfortable than traditional footrests, and whether special contactless sensor system can accurately track how people use their desks and footrests without requiring them to wear extra devices.

If you decide to participate, you will come to our lab on the School of Public Health for a single visit. During this 60–90-minute session, you will use different versions of the footrest and its controller, and complete simple computer tasks such as typing, reading, or word searches. After each trial, we will ask you to answer short questionnaires about your experience. In addition, one 10-minute portion of the session will be videotaped (without recording your face or voice) to help validate the contactless sensor system designed to measure workstation use.

To participate, you must be at least 18 years old, able to speak English, have normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and have prior experience using a sit-stand desk. You cannot participate if you have major mobility limitations or musculoskeletal injuries that would make it difficult to sit, stand, or use a footrest. Your responses will be kept confidential and de-identified, and your feedback will help us improve future ergonomic designs for healthier office work.

Overview

All data will be recorded in Case Report Form and stored in the Texas A&MREDCap System.

The study will take place at the research facility of the Center for Translational Research on Aging and Longevity (CTRAL), Texas A&M University. The study involves 1 screening visit lasting up to 2 hours followed by 6 study days lasting up to 7 hours that can be completed within 4 weeks. Fasting prior to screening is not required.

The PI or appointed research staff will interface with the subject during a screening visit at a convenient time to the subject, in private. Once consent is obtained the participant is screened for eligibility. Participant interview, a personal health history and use of medication will be assessed to determine whether the inclusion/exclusion criteria are met. The subject will be asked to arrive in the fasted state on study days. Subjects will consume 15 servings of the liquid nutrition supplement via sip feeding every 20 minutes for the span of 6 hours. The subjects will be fed the liquid nutritional supplement every 20 minutes for 6 hours. The liquid nutrition supplement will target the amino acid formulation in the following meals (1) total amino acid, (2) Essential Amino Acids (EAA), (3) EAA +  𝛃-hydroxy 𝛃-methylbutyric acid (HMB), (4)  EAA + leucine (LEU), (5) EAA high, and (6) Placebo. Liquid nutrition supplements will be given to subjects according to a randomized and cross-over design. The subjects will receive 6 different meals over the span of the six study days.

Assessing the use of biomarkers to measure children’s reading skills

PI: Steven Woltering, PhD The purpose of the study is to explore the usefulness of biomarkers (e.g., eye movements and brain activity) to measure children’s reading skills (e.g., good reading skill, poor reading skill or diagnosis of dyslexia).
Contact
Juan Quiñonez
  • 9799858406

Overview

The objective of this project is to explore the usefulness of biomarkers (e.g., eye movements and brain activity) to measure children’s reading skills (e.g., good reading skills, poor reading skills, or diagnosis of dyslexia). Our central research question is: which biomarkers (i.e., EEG activity and eye movements) could help improve the identification of dyslexia? The rationale for this project is that identifying biomarkers related to reading difficulties will offer new ways to improve the early identification of children at risk. To do this we will register the eye movements and brain activity of children with and without reading difficulties (dyslexia) while they solve a reading task. We will also assess their reading skill and working memory (visual and verbal) to establish if there is any relationship between these and the results of the experiment. We expect to have 100 participants (50 children with dyslexia and 50 children with an average reading skill) that are currently attending 3rd or 4th grade, and that are fluent in English; without any history of neurological or cognitive impairment, and normal vision.

title.rendered: Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

content.rendered:
1. Home

Evaluating changes in brain functional networks during menopause

PI: Jessica Bernard, PhD This work is seeking to understand how the hormonal changes and fluctuations of perimenopause impact how brain networks are organized, and in turn how hormone therapy may impact these networks and their changes. We are using a technique called dense sampling with brain imaging, where we will take a lot of measurements (24) over time, in a sample of 4 dedicated women, to better understand how this dynamic time of change impacts the brain in middle-aged and older women.
Contact
Jessica Bernard
  • 979-845-2581
  • Jessica.bernard@tamu.edu

Overview

During perimenopause levels of hormones such as estrogen are fluctuating in the body, and this can lead to cognitive dysfunction, including brain fog, which impacts women’s quality of life. The brain relies on large-scale networks – connections among brain areas – to support cognition. Despite growing evidence suggesting estrogen’s role in brain network organization, research on how hormonal fluctuations impact brain connectivity during menopause is limited. Additionally, hormone therapy (HT) remains controversial, with uncertainty about the optimal timing for its initiation to preserve brain health and prevent neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s. This project aims to explore how estrogen fluctuations during menopause impact brain network connectivity and to evaluate the effects of HT on these changes.

Using resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI), a type of brain imaging where participants relax and let their mind wander, we will examine the impact of menopause and HT on the dynamic functional connections in the brain. This study will use dense-sampling approaches (many longitudinal measures on small samples, in this case, 24 measures across 6 months) to investigate fluctuations in brain network connectivity in humans at different menopausal stages (perimenopause and post-menopause), with and without HT. All participants will undergo weekly brain imaging scans scheduled at the participant’s convenience, provide saliva samples at each visit to measure hormones, answer questionnaires related to menopausal symptoms and health, and wear an Oura ring to track sleep, heart rate, body temperature, and movement. Only females will be included in this study, and participation is limited to 4 participants: 2 perimenopausal participants, and 2 post-menopausal participants. One participant in each category will be using HT and the other will not. There are no strict age limits or exclusions, but we expect that all participants will be over the age of 40. Exclusion criteria include left-handedness and any factor that is a contraindication for the brain imaging environment.

Duration

Participants will complete 24 visits. These visits will be once per week over the course of 6 months. 

Compensation

Participants will be compensated $20 per visit. They will also receive a completion bonus of $500 for completing all visits, totally $1000. Finally, participants will be asked to wear an Oura ring for the 6-months of the study. After the study is complete they will be able to keep the ring.

Investigating the effects of estrogen on the efficacy of TMS in improving cognition

PI: Jessica Bernard, PhD This study aims to explore the influence of natural estrogen fluctuations associated with the menstrual cycle on the efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation in enhancing cognition. Participants will undergo neurostimulation, fill out questionnaires, complete cognitive tasks, and provide daily urine samples.
Contact
Casey Delaney
  • caseydelaney@tamu.edu

Overview

Participants will be screened for inclusion based on guidelines for iTBS and provide written informed consent. Participants in the stimulation group will complete two sessions at Day 1 (first day of menses) and around Day 14 of their menstrual cycle (approximating the time of ovulation in an average 28 day menstrual cycle), undergoing stimulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in both sessions. The second visit will be scheduled within Day 12 to Day 16, with Day 14 being optimal if possible. Targeting the location of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex will be done using a template brain and image guidance from the TMS system. The day of the menstrual cycle in which participants attend their first session will be counterbalanced across participants within a group. Participants in the sham group will complete the same sessions at Day 1 and 14 of their cycle, but will receive sham stimulation on both visits. Following neurostimulation, participants will complete various cognitive tasks (described in detail below). These cognitive tasks will be practiced prior to the neurostimulation and randomized across participants. Participants will be asked to take home a Mira hormone monitor and testing strips to collect and test daily urine samples throughout the study. This will range from 14-21 days of collection.

Participants in this study will be right handed English-speaking adult females between the ages of 18 and 35. Right handedness will be  confirmed by the Edinburgh handedness inventory questionnaire. These individuals will be those with regular menstrual cycles and not using any form of hormonal birth control. We will recruit 2 groups of young adults, each with 40 participants, for a total of 80 participants. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the two groups: stimulation or sham. The stimulation group will receive real iTBS stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the sham group will receive sham stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Participants across both groups will be excluded based on safety measures for non-invasive brain stimulation procedures. This may include history of seizure, stroke, or neurological disorder, pregnancy, use of stimulant medications, or the presence of metal or magnetic objects near the head. All participants will complete a safety screening form prior to any study procedures. Due to the nature of the tests used here and the verbal stimuli, all participants will need to be English-speaking as we do not have validated non-English versions of the stimuli at this time.

Two visits, each about 2 hours, completed within two weeks.

The effects of a custom-fitted mouthguard on isometric cervical muscle strength

PI: Steven Riechman, PhD Assessing the effect of custom-fitted mouth guards on neck muscle strength compared to non-fitted mouth guards.
Contact
Edward Williams
  • 830-456-7221
  • Edward.williams@tamu.edu

Overview

The study will include young adults aged 18-35 years that fit the ACSM guidelines of an active individual. Pregnant persons, self-reported history of spinal cord injury, current neck pain, TMJ, chronic pathologies affecting the head/neck, and self-reported concussion or neck injury in the pack 6 months will be excluded. Potential subjects will be recruited through flyers posted on campus, online, or through kinesiology classes. Interested subjects will contact study personnel to schedule an appointment for consent and screening. After consent, subjects will be screened to ensure they meet all inclusion and exclusion criteria. Once eligibility is determined, enrolled subjects will be fitted for the custom mouthguards and undergo data collection. Visits: Enrolled subjects will be asked to complete two study visits. The first visit will be completed immediately after consent and enrollment. The second visit will be completed between 1-2 weeks after the first visit, depending on scheduling availability. The first visit will consist of consent, enrollment, fitting for the custom mouthguard, and familiarization with the testing procedures. Subject height, weight, neck length, neck circumference, and head circumference will also be recorded. The second visit will be identical to the first, but the mouthguard fitting and anthropometric measurements will not need to be repeated.

Participants’ neck flexion, extension, and lateral flexion maximal isometric strength will be assessed using an in-line tension high sensitivity load cell anchored to the floor and connected to a harness around their head. Neck rotation will be assessed using a handheld dynamometer. Participants will perform 3 submaximal trials for each position as a warm-up. Participants will then be instructed to perform 3 trials of each movement with the cue “pull as hard and fast as you can for 5 seconds at 100%.” To mitigate fatigue, they will be given 30 seconds of rest between trials, 3 minute of rest between positions, and 5 minutes of rest between conditions. The head harness will be positioned across the occiput for extension, the temporal bones for lateral flexion, and the forehead for flexion. The participants will be positioned prone on a padded table for extension, side-lying for lateral flexion, and supine for flexion. The participants torso and shoulders will be secured with seat belts to prevent additional contributions from those structures. For rotation, subjects will be seated next to a wall with a handheld dynamometer positioned between their temporal bone and the wall. They will be instructed to “push as hard and fast as you can for 5 seconds at 100%.” The rest protocols will also be 30 seconds between trials and 1 minute between positions. Measures from each mouthguard will be standardized across trials and conditions.

Two total visits within 3 weeks of each other. Each visit will last about one hour.

This study aims to investigate the extent to which bilingual teachers’ social-emotional competencies (SEC) predict burnout, particularly emotional exhaustion, and their intention to leave the teaching profession. Participants will include certified or in-training bilingual and general education teachers working in kindergarten through 12th grade within Texas school districts. Teachers from a variety of school levels—elementary, middle, high school, and alternative placements—will be invited to participate. These surveys will take approximately 25 minutes to complete. Inclusion criteria require participants to be currently employed as bilingual or general education teachers in Texas, and they must have access to the internet to complete the survey. Overview

The objective of this project is to explore the usefulness of biomarkers (e.g., eye movements and brain activity) to measure children’s reading skills (e.g., good reading skills, poor reading skills, or diagnosis of dyslexia). Our central research question is: which biomarkers (i.e., EEG activity and eye movements) could help improve the identification of dyslexia? PI: Edgar Rojas-Muñoz
PhD, Industrial Engineering, Purdue University This study evaluates how AR wearables support safety and user awareness during industrial tasks in hazardous settings, focusing on three safety features: adaptive interfaces (A1), real-time hazard detection (A2), and behavior monitoring (A3). Overview

The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of safety-preserving capabilities of augmented reality (AR) wearable devices during the performance of industrial tasks in hazardous environments. The study aims to produce a technical report outlining the results on safety and user awareness across three safety-preserving capability approaches: (A1) Environment and Context-Aware Adaptive User Interfaces, (A2) Real-Time Estimation of Safety Hazards in an Industrial Setting, and (A3) Real-Time Estimation of Unsafe Behavior.

The experiment will be conducted over four separate sessions, estimated to last over a month and a half. The sessions will require participants to conduct 4 different types of industrial tasks (Surveying, Inspecting, Measuring, and Interacting). They will then be asked to evaluate their experience for the different conditions presented in the sessions. The first session is mandatory, while the following sessions are optional. The inclusion criteria encompasses being 18 years of age or older, being proficient in the English language, not having a significant medical condition, not having some vision impairments that require the use of glasses (contacts are fine), and not having a history of seizures.

Overview

We intend to calibrate the magnitudes of four sets of linguistic amplifiers in Chinese and Farsi. Volunteers must be a native speakers of one of these. The calibrated amplifiers will be used in subsequent studies to construct questionnaire response continua for labeled magnitude scales (LMS). This study, followed by future validity studies, will yield measures of immediate experiences that are usable by researchers and managers with approximately 1/3 of the world’s population. The linguistic amplifiers to be calibrated follow: 

  1. Amplifiers of Intensity: Not at all, Slightly, Somewhat, Quite, Very, Greatly, As Much as Possible

The role of anxiety and depression on cognitive flexibility

PI: Joseph M. Orr The most prevalent mood disorders, anxiety, and depression, have been empirically associated with impaired cognitive flexibility and decision-making. Some studies report increased flexibility under moderate levels of anxiety; therefore the link between anxiety, depression, and cognitive flexibility is not clear. The current study will examine how cognitive flexibility is impacted in anxiety and depression by assessing pupil and gaze responses to task information(eye tracking).
Contact
Juan Balcazar
  • balc557@tamu.edu

Overview

Cognitive flexibility, or the ability to adaptively switch between multiple activities or task sets, is often considered a core aspect of executive functioning. In laboratory settings, flexibility is often operationalized using task switching paradigms, whereby participants switch between simple tasks such as color or letter categorization. While traditionally, task switching relied on cues or fixed task orders to instruct task choice, more recently, voluntary task switching (VTS) paradigms which allow participants to choose when and how frequently to switch between two possible tasks. Our work has shown that individuals favor repeating tasks compared to switching and switch less across the experiment. Our previous work has investigated brain and pupil responses in healthy adults; however, recent work has shown that mood and affect influence flexibility. The most prevalent mood disorders, anxiety, and depression, have been empirically associated with impaired cognitive flexibility and decision-making. Importantly, in task-switching, hyper-vigilant states in anxiety lead to more errors, and ruminative states in depression lead to slow reaction times. Some studies report increased flexibility under moderate levels of anxiety; therefore the link between anxiety, depression, and cognitive flexibility is not clear. Further, a known marker of anxiety and depression is aberrant processing of negative feedback– which influences flexibility and future decision-making. Therefore, the current study will examine how cognitive flexibility is impacted in anxiety and depression by assessing pupil and gaze responses to task information.(eye tracking).

When participants arrive to the lab, they will be ushered to a private testing room to sign a consent form. Following consent, participants will be asked to verify via a screening form that they have no photosensitive epilepsy or have a pacemaker or implanted cardioverter defibriliator or require the use of a medical device that may be impacted by infrared light emitted from the eye tracking device. Answers will be recorded in Redcap, a secure web application. 

Participants who have a history of photosensitive epilepsy will be excluded because the eye tracking camera has infrared illuminators that flash and could induce sensation in those with photosensitive epilepsy. Participants who have a pacemaker will be excluded because the eye tracking camera is mounted with a magnet that could interfere with pacemakers if held against the chest. Participants with a medical device whose function could be impeded by the infrared illuminators from the eye-tracker will be excluded.

This study will be conducted in older adults with and without chronic diseases and frailty. PI: Jeffrey Gagne, Ph.D. The overall goal of this research program is to broadly delineate the socio-emotional, cognitive, and educational implications of COVID-19 in preschoolers. We will also assess parent, family, and teacher factors such as personality, emotionality, health and mental health, socioeconomic status, family/school environment, parenting style, and major life events (in the context of COVID-19). 
Contact
Jeffrey Gagne
  • jeffgagne@tamu.edu

Overview

The overall goal of this research program is to broadly delineate the socio-emotional, cognitive, and educational implications of COVID-19. Specifically, we will also assess parent, family, and teacher factors such as personality, emotionality, health and mental health, socioeconomic status, family/school environment, parenting style, and major life events (in the context of COVID-19). One goal of our study will be to explore how changes in financial stress and major life events/stressors could affect children’s adjustment in preschool and eventually across the school transition.

Research questions:

1.         Investigate socio-emotional and cognitive development in preschool children focusing on SC, BI and related emotional and cognitive variables and health and education outcomes. Do major life events/stressors associated with COVID-19 magnify negative effects on the physical and mental health and learning trajectories of preschool children?

2.         Examine how the pandemic affects the relationships children have with their parents, siblings, peers, and teachers.

3.         Employing a socio-economically, racially and ethnically diverse sample, which children and families are most at- risk and which are most resilient?Preschool is an important stage of socio-emotional and cognitive development that has significant ramifications for school readiness and transition. During the COVID-19 pandemic, preschoolers and their families are experiencing myriad interruptions and stressors that affect outcomes. In particular, self-control (SC) and behavioral inhibition (BI; inhibited/withdrawn behavior in the presence of strangers or novel situations) are two aspects of socio- emotional and cognitive development that emerge early in life and show substantial individual differences by late toddlerhood that may be influenced by COVID-19 conditions. Both SC and BI are associated with behavioral and academic maladjustment that can extend through childhood and adolescence. Low SC is linked to externalizing behavior problems and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and high BI is a risk factor for anxiety disorders. The CDC estimates that 9.4% of U.S. children 2-17 years of age have a lifetime ADHD diagnosis (6.1 million children) and 7% of children aged 3-17 years (approximately 4.4 million) have a diagnosed anxiety disorder. Together, anxiety and ADHD affect nearly 11 million children each year and result in substantial economic, academic, and psychological burdens for children and families. In fact, by 2030, mental disorders are expected to comprise more than a third of the global economic burden of disease – more than cancer, diabetes, and respiratory illnesses combined. A critical period for the manifestation of symptoms and diagnosis of these disorders is during transition to formal schooling (National Institute for Early Education Research, 2016). Despite their overlapping development and subsequent influence on behavioral maladjustment and school outcomes, there are notably few studies that examine the etiology of SC and BI and pathways to long-term academic achievement and social development. Some children with low SC or high BI develop problems; others do not. Moreover, some may present with both high BI and low SC, an understudied typology given traditional divisions in developmental research. The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic offers an opportunity to study these aspects of socio- emotional and cognitive development in a rare but important context. The overall goals of this investigation are to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms by which SC and BI are associated with typical and atypical social, emotional, and cognitive development across the school transition under COVID-19 conditions.

Participants must be 18 years of age or older, fluent in English, must not wear glasses (contacts are fine), and cannot have photosensitive epilepsy. Evaluating the Perception of Eye Contact in Mixed Reality

PI: Edgar J. Rojas-Muñoz, PhD This study examines how variations in fixation points relative to a camera affect perceived eye contact quality in Mixed Reality (MR) environments using a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task with pre-recorded video pairs. Overview

This study investigates the detectability threshold of perceived eye contact quality in Mixed Reality (MR) settings, focusing on how variations in fixation points relative to a camera impact this perception. Participants will wear an MR headset and engage in a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task, viewing pairs of pre-recorded videos displayed on a virtual panel. In each pair, the participant will choose the video that gives the better perception of eye contact. The study consists of two conditions: a controlled environment with a neutral background (Condition 1) and a dynamic work environment featuring two individuals and background activity (Condition 2). Condition 1 is further divided into four variables based on iris color and the presence of glasses. Each video in Condition 1 lasts 5 seconds, while those in Condition 2 last 10 seconds. Participants will evaluate eye contact by responding to prompts after each pair, with breaks between conditions to prevent fatigue. The study is estimated to take 60 minutes, including training and breaks, with minimal physical demand to reduce cybersickness risks.The study aims to recruit approximately 200 participants, ensuring diversity across gender and ethnic backgrounds. Eligible participants must be 18 years or older and proficient in English to effectively follow instructions and respond to prompts. The human cerebellum: a novel target for cognitive & motor interventions in aging & Alzheimer’s Disease

PI: Dr. Jessica Bernard, PhD This study will focus on the central prediction that the cerebellum is an optimal target for remediation of cognitive function in aging, and in neurodegenerative disease. This will test the hypothesis that if the cerebellum is a key target, then there will be improvements in motor and cognitive behavior, brain connectivity, and functional activation after non-invasive stimulation.
Contact
Jerilyn James
  • jerilyn.james@tamu.edu

Overview

The proposed work has been designed to maximize the knowledge gained and scientific output from our participants by combining non-invasive brain stimulation (in this instance, intermittent theta burst stimulation, iTBS) with multimodal neuroimaging. We will recruit 3 groups of adults, each with 40 participants (120 total). Young adults will be between the ages of 18 and 30 years. We will also recruit cognitively normal (CN) older adults over the age of 60 and with a score on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA) of over 26. Finally, we will recruit older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI; again, over the age of 60) as defined by a score of 26 or lower on the MOCA. Additional exclusion criteria are applicable across all three groups and relate to safety measures put into place for the neuroimaging and non-invasive brain stimulation procedures. Due to the general lack of knowledge and understanding of the cerebellum in cognitive decline more broadly, we will develop our foundational understanding of the cerebellum in cognitive decline in those with MCI, and future work will extend to include individuals with AD. It is also notable that intervention in those with MCI may have longer term positive impacts, with respect to quality of life and both cognitive and motor outcomes.        

All participants will complete two sessions as part of this investigation. The general procedures will remain the same, with the exception of the stimulation procedures. Participants will receive both real and sham stimulation in counterbalanced order. We will use a single-blind procedure, and the stimulation order will be revealed after the completion of all study procedures. All participants will be carefully screened for inclusion consistent with guidelines for iTBS and neuroimaging. After providing informed consent (or assent for individuals with MCI that may not have capacity for direct consent) participants will complete two sessions. They will undergo both real and sham cerebellar stimulation. The order of these sessions will be counterbalanced across participants within a group, and participants will be blinded to the conditions until after study completion. The stimulation session will be immediately followed by neuroimaging. The neuroimaging scan will take approximately 90 minutes during which all participants will complete a resting state functional scan to quantify functional brain networks, several behavioral paradigms to quantify cerebellar function and organization across groups, a high-resolution structural scan for both analysis and for quantification of cerebellar volume, and finally a diffusion tensor imaging scan to quantify white matter tracts connecting the cerebellum to the cerebral cortex. For all behavioral tasks completed in the scanner, we will use varying stimuli between sessions to limit the impact of practice effects on our findings.

Traumatic stress Risk factors And Daily Symptoms (TRiADS)

PI: Brian Albanese PhD The present study will evaluate several potential biobehavioral processes underlying PTSD vulnerability and extend this work to understanding the naturalistic experience of PTSD symptoms by using real-time ecological momentary assessment (EMA) assessments.
Contact
Daniela Porro
  • danielaporro@tamu.edu

Overview

Although experiencing traumatic events is common, only a minority experience lasting symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). In this study, we seek to better understand neural mechanisms underlying PTSD symptomology, particularly why some individuals experience greater re-experiencing and engage in more avoidance behaviors in response to stress or trauma reminders. Participants will come into the lab for a variety of tasks indexing emotional responding, cognitive control, and decision making while we record the electrical brain activity using a safe and non-invasive method called electroencephalography (EEG). Participants will then complete an ecological momentary assessment (EMA) period where they will complete brief (2-3 minute) surveys on their smart phone 4 times per day for 14 days. Following this, participants will complete a clinical interview and self-report measures at a 3 month follow up appointment. During the follow up periods, we are examining the relationship between neurobehavioral mechanisms and real-world functioning.

The participant population for the current project will be undergraduate students at Texas A&M University from the SONA subject pool (Psychological and Brain Sciences) and community members from the Bryan/ College Station area. A single group consisting of trauma exposed individuals (n=150, aged 18-65, English speaking, history of trauma exposure, endorsing intrusion and/or avoidance PTSS symptom(s) in the past month will be included.) Participants are invited for a CAPS-5, SCID-5-RV and Joiner SRA interview based on PCL-5 > 32 (a measure of PTSD).

Prandial Metabolic Phenotyping in Sarcopenic Older Adults Comparing Plant Based and Whey Based Protein

PI: Dr. Nicolaas Deutz, MD, PhD To observe the metabolic effect of plant-based protein versus dairy based protein in older adults.
Contact
Dr. Nicolaas Deutz or Research Staff
  • 979-422-1789
  • research@ctral.org

Overview

The study will be conducted in sarcopenic and non-sarcopenic older adults, stratified into different age categories. A sip feeding model will be used as it is a good model to establish the anabolic capacity of meals {Jonker, 2018, 17-31}. We hypothesize that plant-based protein induces less protein anabolism, due to lower production of EAA and higher production of non-essential amino acids (NEAA) as compared to dairy protein. The NEAA kinetics will be different between the plant proteins as soy protein has relative high levels of the NEAA arginine {Deutz, 1998, 2435-45} and Pea protein of aspartate/glutamate {Salles, 2021 #16377}. Our results will guide future nutritional advice on replacing daily protein with plant based proteins while keeping the overall effects on metabolism comparable for both the EAA and NEAA.

The study will take place at the research facility of the Center for Translational Research on Aging and Longevity (CTRAL), Texas A&M University located in the Human Clinical Research Building) affiliated with Texas A&M University. The study involves 1 screening visit of approx. 3 hours, and 4 study days. Some study procedures (e.g., body composition, skeletal muscle function, questionnaires) may be skipped if completed within the past 3 months at CTRAL. All data will be recorded in Case Report Form and stored in the Texas A&M REDCap System. Inclusion criteria: 50-95 years old, stable body weight for the past 3 months, ability to walk, sit down, and stand up, willingness to lay supine in bed for up to 6 hours. Exclusion criteria: Established diagnosis and active treatment of chronic disease: Insulin dependent diabetes mellitus, active malignancy, heart disease, kidney disease, liver disease, HIV/AIDS, Asthma (moderate to severe), Hep (A,B, or C), known allergy to any of the components of the feeding (soy, pea, or whey – dairy), established daily diet of vegetarian / vegan composition, or any condition according to the PI or nurse that was found during the screening visit, that would interfere with the study or safety of the patient.

Duration

This study will include 1 screening visit (~3 hours) and a maximum of 4 study visits (~6 hours).

Evaluation of biomarkers for predicting macronutrient intake

PI: Nicolaas Deutz, MD, PhD This study will develop new methods important for precision nutrition by measuring the response of both glucose and amino acids in the body to a variety of real pre-defined meals.
Contact
Laura Ruebush
  • 979-422-1789
  • research@ctral.org

Overview

You may be familiar with continuous glucose monitors (or CGMs) commonly worn by those with diabetes or seen on commercials. These are small devices that monitor glucose levels of the body on a 24-hour basis and link to software for you to monitor the levels in real-time without painful finger pricks. The purpose of this study is to work alongside engineers to create the next generation of this device. Instead of only looking at glucose, we will also be looking at amino acids. By studying the metabolism of amino acids and how the body uses them, we can better understand the maintenance of muscles since amino acids make up proteins and proteins make up muscle.

To be eligible for this study you must be between the ages of 50 and 75 (inclusive) with a body mass index (BMI) between 25 and 35 (inclusive). You can estimate your BMI here. If you are interested in the study, you will start with an initial screening visit to meet the study team and learn more about the procedures. If you are eligible, you will be scheduled for 4 additional study days that will last about 14 hours. On the study days we ask you to come in the morning fasted, we will provide you with 2 carefully created and very yummy meals, and in the evenings you will be sent home with a goodie bag of snacks. During the day you will have two devices attached, an IV collecting blood samples from one arm, and a catheter in the other arm collecting fluid samples from outside the blood called interstitial fluid. Because the study days are longer than usual, you will have up to 6 weeks to complete these 4 study days, and you can do a maximum of 2 visits in one week.

Integration of Cognitive Processing Therapy and Relapse Prevention for Alcohol Use Disorder and Co-Occurring PTSD: A Randomized Clinical Trial

PIs: Anka Vujanovic, PhD (Texas A&M University) and Sudie Back, PhD (Medical University of South Carolina) The PATH (PTSD & Alcohol Use Treatment & Healing) study will compare two forms of talk therapy with individuals who have experienced a traumatic event and drink alcohol. We offer both telehealth and in-person options for all study visits.
Contact
Kat Roberts (PATH Study Coordinator)
  • (979) 458-9153 or (854) 253-9987
  • path@tamu.edu

Overview

PATH (PTSD & Alcohol Use Treatment & Healing) was created to develop more effective treatments for individuals with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and alcohol-related problems. PTSD is one of the most common conditions among individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD). In fact, approximately 50% of those with PTSD also have AUD.

The PATH program will compare two forms of talk therapy to learn which form of treatment works best, for whom, and the mechanisms underlying improvements. These two forms of talk therapy include 1) standard care (Relapse Prevention) or 2) a new treatment that combines Relapse Prevention with Cognitive Processing Therapy for PTSD. Both interventions involve evidence-based therapy with a trained clinician.

PATH is funded by the National Institute of Health (NIH). This study is led by Dr. Sudie Back at the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC) and Dr. Anka Vujanovic at Texas A&M University (TAMU). Both are licensed clinical psychologists with over 30 years combined experience in clinical research and expertise in co-occurring PTSD and alcohol use conditions.

Duration

Baseline assessment (3 hours) 12 treatment sessions (1.5 hours each) 3 follow up visits (2 hours each)

Compensation

Up to $560 for completing all study components, including a baseline assessment, 12 therapy sessions across 6 weeks, and 3 follow up assessments at 3-, 6-, and 12-months after the therapy phase.
